blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A counter in the innermost statement of a report builder reads 30,000 at 500 customers, 120,000 at 1,000 and 480,000 at 2,000. Production has 16,000 customers. What does that predict there?

options.text: About 31 million, since the count has grown fourfold at each doubling, and three more doublings multiply it by 64
options.says: a ratio of 4 per doubling is quadratic growth; 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 times 480,000

options.text: About 3.8 million, since the fourfold step at each doubling is a constant factor, and Big O drops constant factors
options.says: the constant Big O drops multiplies every count alike; a ratio that repeats at each doubling is the growth itself

options.text: About 4.3 million, since a ratio near four at small sizes falls toward two at large ones, as it does for a sort
options.says: the n log n ratio is 2 x (1 + 1/log2 n), close to 2 already at n = 1,000; a steady 4.00 is quadratic

options.text: About 3.8 million, since the quadratic part of a count shows at small sizes and the linear part takes over at large ones
options.says: the highest-order term is the one that dominates as n grows, which is why Big O keeps it

origin.section: Count the Operations: Doubling n Shows the Order

questions.stem: For each request a permissions service copies a role's permission names into a new ArrayList and calls retainAll(granted), where granted is a List<String> of the user's grants. Both hold about 5,000 names in the load test and 40,000 in production. How much longer does one call take in production?

options.text: About 8 times, since retainAll is one bulk operation that walks each of the two lists once
options.says: ArrayList.retainAll calls granted.contains for every element it holds, so the walk over granted happens once per element

options.text: About 8 times, since ArrayList.contains reads its backing array by index, in constant time
options.says: get(i) is constant time; contains compares the argument with each element in turn, which is linear

options.text: About 64 times, since retainAll checks every name against the other list, and each of those checks is a scan
options.says: n calls of an O(n) contains is O(n^2): eight times the names, sixty-four times the comparisons

options.text: About 64 times, since retainAll's receiver is copied into a growing array, and each growth copies the whole list
options.says: even an array grown one name at a time copies only a small multiple of n elements in total, since it grows by half; the 64 comes from the contains calls retainAll makes

origin.section: A Call Inside a Loop Multiplies: List.contains in a Loop Is O(n²)

questions.stem: An event recorder appends to one new ArrayList<>() for a whole trading day, about 3,000,000 events. A latency monitor shows almost every append taking tens of nanoseconds, and a handful during the day taking milliseconds. What explains the slow ones?

options.text: The slow appends each copied the list into a larger array, since the array grows by half its size each time it fills
options.says: with capacity + capacity/2 growth about thirty copies cover millions of adds, and the last few each copy hundreds of thousands of references

options.text: The slow appends each copied the list into a larger array, since the array grows by a fixed number of slots each time it fills
options.says: ArrayList grows by half its capacity, not by a fixed step; a fixed step is what makes the total copying O(n^2)

options.text: The slow appends were pauses caused elsewhere, since amortised constant time means that every append costs the same
options.says: amortised constant is an average over many adds; the add that grows the array copies every element

options.text: The slow appends were pauses caused elsewhere, since each append allocates a new node that the garbage collector later reclaims
options.says: an ArrayList add that finds room allocates nothing; the probe measured 0 bytes for every add but the 30 that grew the array

origin.section: Amortised O(1): ArrayList.add Copies Each Element a Few Times, Not n Times

questions.stem: A payment validator checks each request's currency against List.of("EUR", "USD", "GBP", "CHF", "JPY", "SEK"). In review, someone asks for a HashSet instead, because contains on a list is O(n). Which reading of the comment is right?

options.text: Big O doesn't rank the two here, since the list never gets longer, so each check costs the same however many requests arrive
options.says: Big O describes growth with n; with n fixed, constants decide, and they have to be measured

options.text: Big O doesn't rank the two here, since List.of builds a hashed list, so each check is a hash lookup however long the list is
options.says: contains on a List.of(...) scans: it called equals once per element for a code it didn't hold

options.text: Big O favours the set here, since its lookup does not depend on n, so it beats a scan once the list holds more than one element
options.says: Big O says nothing about which code is faster at a given n; it only compares growth, and with the list's length fixed there is no growth to compare

options.text: Big O favours the set here, since the list is scanned on every request, so its cost grows with the number of requests
options.says: n is the list's length, not the traffic; a missing code costs six equals calls however many requests arrive

origin.section: At Small n, Constants and the Cache Decide

concepts: ArrayList.removeAll and retainAll call contains on their argument for each element, so with a List argument they are O(n^2).

At small n the constant costs Big O drops can make the higher-order code faster, as insertion sort beat merge sort up to 512 elements on one machine; for a fixed small n Big O does not rank the choices.
Counting the innermost operation at n and 2n gives the order: a ratio of 2 is linear, about 2.2 is n log n, 4 is quadratic; Big O keeps that growth and drops constant factors.
Amortised O(1) is an average: the add that grows an ArrayList copies every element, so a large list has rare, large pauses; presizing removes them.
